title: The Declaration of Independence
hook: It's remembered for 'life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness' — but most of the Declaration is a long list of grievances: a case that a government had broken faith with the governed.
key_points: Adopted July 4, 1776, it announced the thirteen American colonies' separation from British rule.
Its philosophical core: governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed, to secure rights all people hold.
If a government becomes destructive of those ends, the document argues, the people may alter or abolish it.
The bulk of the text is a list of specific grievances against the King — evidence offered to justify revolt.
Many grievances centered on accountability: arbitrary power, a judiciary bent to the ruler's will, officials beyond the people's reach.
It is not itself law — the Constitution is — but it set the founding ideals later documents tried to make real.
content_html: The Declaration of Independence is quoted for a single soaring line about equality and unalienable rights. But as historian Robert Parkinson writes in The Conversation — marking its 250th anniversary — the document is mostly something more pointed: a carefully built case for why a people may overthrow their government.
extra_html: Adopted on July 4, 1776, the Declaration announced that the thirteen colonies were separating from British rule. Its opening lays out a theory of government: that governments exist to secure the rights people already hold, that they "derive their just powers from the consent of the governed," and that when a government becomes destructive of those ends, the people have the right to alter or abolish it. Everything after that is evidence. The longest part of the document is a list of grievances against the King — a bill of particulars meant to prove a pattern of abuse serious enough to justify revolution. Parkinson highlights how many of those grievances are really about accountability: arbitrary power, a judiciary bent to the ruler's will, officials placed beyond the reach of the people they governed. The Declaration is not itself the law of the land — that role belongs to the Constitution, written more than a decade later — but it fixed the founding ideals of equality, consent, and accountable government that the new nation would spend centuries trying to live up to. (U.S. founding context.)

source.name: The Conversation
authors: Robert Parkinson, Professor of History, Binghamton University, State University of New York

related.title: The Federalist Papers
related.hook: To sell a skeptical public on the new Constitution, three founders wrote 85 newspaper essays under a single fake name. They're still the best guide to what it means.

related.title: The Social Contract
related.hook: Why should anyone obey the state? The social contract answers: people trade some freedom for the security and order that only collective authority can provide.

related.title: The Enlightenment & Modern Politics
related.hook: The radical idea that legitimate power comes from the people — not God or birth — was forged in the Enlightenment, and it still underpins democracy today.

related.title: What Government Is For
related.hook: Every society needs a way to make and enforce collective decisions — that shared system of authority is what we call government.

flashcards.prompt: According to the Declaration of Independence, where do a government's 'just powers' come from?

choices.text: The wealth and lands of the ruler

flashcards.explanation_html: The Declaration holds that governments are instituted to secure people's rights and derive their just powers from the consent of the governed.

flashcards.prompt: What makes up most of the text of the Declaration of Independence?
flashcards.back_html: A detailed list of grievances against the King — evidence presented to justify the colonies' decision to break away.

flashcards.prompt: What did many of the Declaration's grievances have in common?

choices.text: They charged the ruler with unaccountable, arbitrary power beyond the people's reach
They demanded lower taxes and nothing more
They asked the King to expand the colonies' territory

flashcards.explanation_html: As historian Robert Parkinson notes, grievances like a partisan judiciary and officials beyond popular reach all point to a failure of accountability.

flashcards.prompt: Is the Declaration of Independence the foundational *law* of the United States?

choices.text: No — it stated founding ideals; the Constitution is the governing law
Yes — courts apply it as binding law today
Yes — it replaced the Constitution in 1787

flashcards.explanation_html: The Declaration set out principles like equality and consent; the later Constitution is the document that actually structures and binds government.
